Full DiDi Two-Tracker Evaluation and Failure-Clip Review

This analysis evaluates existing predictions only. Neither tracker was rerun, and no subsequent ground truth (GT) was provided to either model. All 180 sequences and 274,882 frames are included, with 360 prediction trajectories across the two models. Of these, 179 sequences were processed in this batch; leaves reuses the earlier results.

1. Overall results

ModelQuality Q ↑Accuracy A ↑Robustness R ↑
DAM4SAM0.68600.71730.9436
SAMURAI0.67930.72070.9319

The mean Q difference, SAMURAI−DAM4SAM, is -0.0066 (-0.66 percentage points). In per-sequence comparisons, DAM4SAM scores higher on 102 sequences and SAMURAI on 78; 0 sequences differ by no more than 1e−6.

A paired sequence bootstrap over these 180 sequences (10,000 resamples, seed=20261027) gives a 95% percentile interval of [-0.0288, +0.0159] for the mean Q difference. This describes exploratory variation within the current fixed collection only. DiDi source sequences may be correlated, so it does not establish a general advantage on independent data.

The median per-sequence difference is -0.0015, and the correlation between the two models’ sequence-level Q scores is 0.755. The mean difference, median, and win/loss counts answer different questions; large-failure sequences must also be examined to understand the overall gap.

2. Unified protocol and comparability

• The primary metrics follow move_didi_results.py and didi-workspace/baseline_experiment.yaml from the pinned DAM4SAM source. Both models use VOT Toolkit 0.7.1. Predicted masks are converted to enclosing bounding boxes; the bytes of the official groundtruth.txt remain unchanged.

• An annotation-file selection issue was identified and corrected: the original archive contains 90 groundtruth_old.txt backup files (86 LaSOT and 4 GOT). By default, VOT gives groundtruth_*.txt higher priority than groundtruth.txt, treating the backups as an object named old. The official GT and backups differ on 5,955 frames, all involving official Special(0) regions versus backup boxes. No valid target geometry annotation was rewritten in this analysis.

• The final data view keeps the original backup files outside the loader directory. All 180 objects were individually verified to use the official groundtruth.txt, with correct lengths and SHA256 hashes matching the original archive. Model outputs, original data, and annotation files were not modified. Results from the default loader are retained in audit-unfiltered-loader and are kept separate from the final results.

• With the backups incorrectly loaded, the earlier Q scores were DAM 0.6816 and SAM 0.6751. The main table in this report contains the final scores using the official GT. This difference comes from the annotation files used for scoring, rather than improvements obtained by rerunning or tuning the models.

• Q uses burnin=0, ignore_unknown=False, and weighted=False; the final aggregation weights sequences equally. The original script converts the first-frame prediction to Special(1), whose scoring behavior is determined by the installed toolkit. This report does not independently exclude the first frame to raise the scores. A measures accuracy on successful frames with positive overlap; R uses a success threshold of IoU>0, which is different from IoU≥0.5.

• The installed implementation has a first-frame edge case: gather_overlaps enters the initialization branch for Special(1). With burnin=0, no frame is removed, and execution does not proceed into the subsequent threshold branch. Therefore, when the first-frame GT is valid, both Q and A may include a zero-overlap first frame. This behavior is preserved here; frame-level diagnostics explicitly exclude the input first frame.

• Both models use the same original DiDi sequences, SAM2.1 Large weights, supplied first-frame segmentation masks, and no intermediate GT corrections. All first-frame masks were rechecked during evaluation. For SAMURAI, this is a comparison under unified mask initialization, rather than a reproduction of its demo’s default box initialization.

• Q/A/R from the official analysis CLI were cross-checked against aggregates obtained by calling the same toolkit version’s functions per sequence; see official-crosscheck.json.

• To avoid retransferring 28GB of images, scoring uses a lightweight data view: the original GT/label bytes are retained, and length/width/height are added to sequence files. Lengths and first-frame dimensions were checked for all 180 sequences. Full images are additionally retained for GOT Val 000014, leaves, and birds2; Q/A/R inputs and valid-frame indices match exactly between the original directories and lightweight view for both models. No synthetic images were substituted for real frames.

• DAM4SAM uses PyTorch 2.1.0 and SAMURAI uses 2.3.1. GPUs include A100, A100 MIG, L40S, and H200. SAMURAI uses a CPU image cache checked through sampled, image-by-image tensor equivalence tests. Prediction quality from these two implementations can be compared, but timing logs should not be interpreted as a strictly controlled speed comparison or an ablation that changes only the memory strategy.

The released data contain multiple GT region types: RECTANGLE on 260,975 frames, SPECIAL on 7,696 frames, and MASK on 6,211 frames. Original mask GT was not silently converted to boxes in this evaluation.

Most unavailable intervals are encoded as Special(0) and skipped under this toolkit protocol. Q therefore does not fully measure absence decisions or false positives during these intervals. A nonempty prediction on a frame without valid annotation cannot automatically be counted as an error. Recovery evaluation should begin when valid annotations resume.

Mean scores across sources are also affected by GT type: the same predicted box may overlap a thin or sparse mask GT less than its enclosing box GT. Consequently, mean-score differences between VOT-derived and LaSOT-derived sequences cannot directly be interpreted as differences in scene difficulty. Representative clips require inspection of the target location and original masks.

Paper reference: Table 2 of the DAM4SAM paper reports Q/A/R of 0.694/0.727/0.944 for SAM2.1++ and 0.680/0.722/0.930 for SAMURAI. These numbers provide context only; numerical proximity is not treated as complete reproduction. The released annotations, versions, and unified initialization used here must be documented. Source: DAM4SAM paper, Table 2.

The current DAM Q is 0.0080 below that table, and SAM Q is 0.0007 below it. These differences have not yet been attributed item by item, so exact reproduction of the paper’s numbers cannot be claimed. The main table provides a unified comparison of the two fixed implementations.

3. Shared difficulties

• Both models have whole-sequence Q below 0.5 on 30 sequences; both have Q below 0.3 on 7 sequences. The 0.5/0.3 cutoffs are screening thresholds used in this analysis, not official categories.

• Both models simultaneously have IoU<0.2 for at least 10 consecutive valid target-present frames on 48 sequences; for at least 30 consecutive frames on 32 sequences.

• After excluding the first frame and frames without valid target-present annotations, there are 266,984 target-present frames. Both models have low overlap simultaneously on 21,565 frames (8.1%).

• Candidates closer to delayed error discovery: both models have mean IoU>0.5 over the 30 frames before failure, followed by shared IoU<0.2 for ≥30 consecutive frames. This identifies 2 sequences / 2 intervals. This establishes the existence of such trajectory patterns, rather than the cause of an identity switch or memory contamination.

• Consecutive low-score intervals are not joined across unknown-GT or target-absent frames. Whether recovery occurs after a low-score interval requires inspection of the subsequent curves. Pixel overlap between a native predicted mask and box GT is not segmentation accuracy; native mask IoU has a direct segmentation interpretation only on sequences with mask GT.

4. Representative clips: observations and limits

Quantitative statistics cover all 180 sequences. Qualitative analysis uses the first frame, key frames before and after failure and within low-score intervals, and local video review of candidate clips. It does not constitute manual frame-by-frame inspection of all 274,882 frames. Video colors show the original mask visualizations: DAM in yellow, SAM in blue, and GT in cyan; leaves reuses the earlier visualization with pink on both sides. Clip-selection thresholds were used only for retrieval and did not affect predictions.

Switching from the specified shoe to the other shoe: VOT2022-LT_dancingshoe

DAM Q=0.2065, SAM Q=0.3456; shared low-overlap fraction 36.3%, longest run 330 frames.

In dancingshoe, the target is one of the dancer’s shoes. Starting around frame 1858, both models’ overlap with that target drops markedly. At frames 1894, 1930, and 1960, the cyan GT still identifies the specified shoe, whereas predictions on both sides lie near the other shoe. These frames have valid GT, so missing annotation cannot explain the low scores.

This is a candidate case of identity confusion between similar local targets, suitable for prioritizing delayed-correction experiments: after tracking has switched to the other shoe, supply one correct mask and check whether tracking returns to and stays with the original shoe. The current results contain no memory read/write traces or counterfactual interventions, so they cannot establish which memory channel caused the failure.

Full video · Representative clip

Persistent tracking of the wrong similar wild boar: LaSOT_pig-18

DAM Q=0.1821, SAM Q=0.2655; shared low-overlap fraction 64.2%, longest run 1036 frames.

The first frame of pig-18 specifies one wild boar. After the two animals approach, overlap, and change their relative positions, the predictions separate from the cyan box. At frame 1280, GT clearly covers the animal on the left, while both models’ nonempty predictions mainly cover the other animal on the right. Later key frames also show disagreement between the predictions and specified target.

This is closer to persistent acceptance of the wrong object as the target than to an empty prediction, and can serve as a case involving an external, similar distractor. Grass occlusion, visible portions, and box boundaries also affect IoU; identity judgments should use the first frame and full video rather than the low-score curve alone.

Full video · Representative clip

Target confusion within a zebra herd: LaSOT_zebra-16

DAM Q=0.2322, SAM Q=0.4342; shared low-overlap fraction 29.7%, longest run 252 frames.

Late in zebra-16, the originally specified zebra approaches neighboring zebras. At frames 811, 937, and 1092, the cyan GT and yellow/blue predictions fall on different animals; some predictions also cover multiple adjacent instances. Both models drift. This is more than a predicted contour being slightly smaller than a box.

This provides a case of external same-class distractors and instance mixing, complementing the local identity confusion in the shoe example. Single-target GT does not assign instance IDs to the other zebras, so rigorous identity-switch counts would require manual instance annotations. The present evidence establishes disagreement with the specified target only.

Full video · Representative clip

Low scores caused by expansion of the target extent: VOT2022-ST_flamingo1

DAM Q=0.1595, SAM Q=0.1051; shared low-overlap fraction 70.0%, longest run 744 frames.

The first-frame target and cyan GT in flamingo1 cover the flamingo’s head. In many subsequent frames, both models’ predictions extend to the neck, body, or even the entire bird, making the predicted enclosing box large relative to the head GT. Similar behavior appears as expansion across multiple train carriages in train-1 and from the hand to the forearm in hand-9.

This is an important counterexample category: shared low Q does not necessarily indicate a cross-object identity switch. Segmentation-granularity bias, local-target retention, and scoring geometry may all contribute. These cases should be treated as a separate category and control, rather than forcing every such low score into a memory-contamination explanation.

Full video · Representative clip

Control: SAMURAI performs substantially better: UTB180_Video_0002

DAM Q=0.2234, SAM Q=0.8906; shared low-overlap fraction 0.0%, longest run 0 frames.

In UTB180_Video_0002, the target fish and a larger fish/shark cross in the image. At frames 337, 367, and 397, SAMURAI’s predicted box still overlaps the cyan GT strongly, while DAM4SAM’s prediction lies in another area or is clearly separated from the target.

This reverse-direction control is retained to avoid selecting only sequences where SAMURAI fails. Overall means cannot replace per-sequence analysis. A new repair method must also be tested for degradation on cases that were already tracked correctly.

Full video · Representative clip

Control: divergence after valid annotations resume: LaSOT_car-17

DAM Q=0.7945, SAM Q=0.1141; shared low-overlap fraction 2.6%, longest run 18 frames.

In car-17, the official GT marks an interval as unavailable; this analysis does not count that interval as failure. At frame 2145, when valid annotations resume, DAM4SAM has high overlap with the target box, while SAMURAI remains clearly displaced. There is also a marked difference at the earlier frame 1977, which has valid GT.

This is a control for differences in recovery behavior. It motivates inspecting both methods’ states before and after target loss, but the current results cannot attribute the difference to motion gating, memory updates, or other implementation factors. Correct scoring must first exclude intervals without valid GT.

Full video · Representative clip

5. Implications for the research direction

A priority research question is how to recover after the correct object has already been lost and correct evidence arrives late. However, the current trajectories without intervention only identify natural clips worth testing. They do not establish which kind of memory received erroneous information, or whether clearing pointers, spatial memory, or replay will work. Without model confidence, memory read/write records, and explicit IDs for additional objects, low IoU alone cannot establish a high-confidence identity switch.

dancingshoe is the recommended starting point: it has a clearly specified shoe and a similar distracting shoe, together with a verifiable interval of shared drift. Next, use pig-18 and zebra-16 to examine confusion with external same-class instances. Treat flamingo1, hand-9, and train-1 as target-extent expansion cases, avoiding their inclusion in a single identity-contamination conclusion.

The next step should fix a development subset from manually reviewed natural clips and give both models the same correct mask at the same delayed-correction frame. Compare correcting only the current mask, clearing suspicious history, restoring a trusted state, and selective repair. Predictions before correction remain unchanged; only current and future outputs are evaluated, alongside degradation on normal clips and additional cost. These interventions have not begun in this analysis.

The annotation conditions must be stated in advance: most DiDi sequences provide per-frame boxes and a first-frame mask only, so subsequent boxes cannot be called precise GT masks. Correction masks can be manually annotated for a small set of development events, or a unified box-correction protocol can be defined separately. The source of external correction evidence during training/testing must also be defined separately from automatic error detection. Oracle diagnostics must not be presented as results of an automatic method without GT.

DiDi is a stress test for distractor scenarios. Findings can guide method development, but subsequent main results still require separate development/test splits and more general datasets. Sequences already used to select cases should be labeled exploratory development data, rather than repeatedly tuned on and then presented as unseen test evidence.
